levels.title: Recipients, means, and motion: cases that carry a conversation

units.title: Whom you give it to and what you use: dative and instrumental in action

lessons.title: The dative for the recipient: whom you give, write, or speak to
lessons.explanation: You have already handed one object to one person with a dative ending (lesson 34). This lesson makes that ending productive for every noun, so the recipient slot stops being a memorised phrase. Compare two sentences that differ only in role. Я читаю книгу (ya chee-TA-yu KNEE-goo) — I am reading a book: книгу is the thing acted on, the accusative direct object. Я пишу маме (ya pee-SHOO MA-mye) — I am writing to mum: маме is the person who receives, and Russian marks a recipient with the dative case. The endings are short and predictable. Masculine and neuter nouns add -у, spelled -ю after a soft stem: брат (brat) — brother becomes брату (BRA-too); учитель (oo-CHEE-tyel) — teacher becomes учителю (oo-CHEE-tye-lyu). Feminine nouns in -а swap that -а for -е: мама (MA-ma) — mum becomes маме; Анна (AN-na) — Anna becomes Анне. Feminine names in -ия take -ии: Мария (ma-REE-ya) — Maria becomes Марии (ma-REE-ee). Every gender takes -ам, or -ям after a soft stem, in the plural: друзьям (drooz-YAM) — to friends. The pronouns are learned as a closed set, each with its own stressed shape: Мне (MNYE) to me, Тебе (tee-BYE) to you, Ему (ye-MOO) to him, Ей (YEY) to her, Нам (NAM) to us, Вам (VAM) to you, Им (EEM) to them. Spanish offers a genuine bridge here: le escribo a mi mamá uses a clitic le plus a, and мне and ему sit in exactly that slot. The difference is that Spanish keeps the extra preposition and Russian does not, so the ending alone must carry the meaning.
lessons.example: Take one verb, пишу (PEE-shoo) I write, and change only the person. Я пишу маме (ya pee-SHOO MA-mye) — I am writing to mum, where мама changes its ending. Я пишу брату (ya pee-SHOO BRA-too) — I am writing to my brother, where брат gains -у. Я пишу друзьям (ya pee-SHOO drooz-YAM) — I am writing to my friends, plural dative. Now add a thing and watch two cases stand in one clause: Я дала маме книгу (ya da-LA MA-mye KNEE-goo) — I gave mum a book. English would allow the same order, and Spanish would say le di un libro a mamá; in the Russian sentence маме is dative because she receives, and книгу is accusative because it is handed over. Read each pair slowly with the marked stress, then at normal speed, and name the recipient aloud before you say the ending: the naming step, not the sound, is what keeps the two cases apart.
lessons.question: Why is Я звоню брату (ya zva-NYOO BRA-too) — I am phoning my brother correct, while Я звоню брата is not?
lessons.answer: The verb звонить to phone governs the dative for the person phoned, so the brother takes the dative ending -у.
lessons.distractor: Брат is animate, so an animate noun in object position must take the genitive-shaped accusative.
lessons.correction: Animacy changes the shape of an accusative object (lesson 51), but the brother here is not an object of the accusative kind at all. Some verbs hand a person straight into the dative slot: звонить to phone, помогать to help, отвечать to answer. The test is the verb, not the animacy of the noun: ask what case this verb wants for a person, then supply that ending. Звонить wants the dative, so the form is брату regardless of how animate the brother is.

depth.definitions: The dative is the case of the recipient, the beneficiary, and the person affected by a state rather than by an action. It is the case label Russian grammars attach to the -u/-e family of endings and to the pronoun set мне, тебе, ему, ей, нам, вам, им. A direct object is the thing or person a verb acts on; an indirect object is the person for whom the action happens, and in Russian that second role is what the dative marks. Verb government is the property of a verb that fixes the case of the noun it takes; it must be learned per verb because it does not follow from meaning.
depth.mechanism: Russian marks the recipient inside the noun rather than in a prepositional phrase, so the information English and Spanish put in word order or particles lives in the ending. Cornell's dative page groups the endings by declension: -у for the zero-ending masculine and o-declension nouns, -е for the a-declension, -ии for feminine -ия nouns, and -ам/-ям in the plural for all declensions. Two consequences deserve stating. First, the dative singular of a feminine -а noun is spelled -е, exactly like the prepositional singular of the same noun: маме is the shape the ending takes in both cases, and only the verb or the preposition tells you which case you are in — пишу маме to mum against думаю о маме about mum. Second, the dative plural can never be confused with the accusative plural, which means plural recipients are where a beginner's dative is most audible and least risky.
depth.secondExample: Move the same recipient through three verbs to see that the ending travels with the noun, not with the verb's meaning: Я помогаю сестре (ya pa-ma-GA-yu sees-TRYE) — I help my sister; Я отвечаю сестре (ya at-vee-CHA-yu sees-TRYE) — I answer my sister; Я показываю сестре фотографии (ya pa-KA-zy-va-yu sees-TRYE fa-ta-GRA-fee-ee) — I show my sister the photographs. The last sentence contains a dative recipient (сестре) and an accusative thing (фотографии) at the same time, which is the shape most Russian transactions take. Notice as well that сестра loses its -а and does not keep a separate possessive word: Russian normally prefers сестре to моей сестре when context is clear.
depth.mistake: Three errors recur. The first uses the accusative for a person because English and Spanish make the person look like a direct object: Я помогаю сестру, where сестре is required. The second imports the Spanish preposition and writes к маме for a plain recipient, which changes the meaning toward movement in the direction of someone. The third over-applies the -е ending to masculine nouns, producing пишу брате. Diagnose by naming the verb first and asking which case it governs, then checking the noun's gender before writing a single letter; if the role analysis is right and only the ending is wrong, record this as a form-retrieval gap rather than a case confusion.
depth.application: Optional practice: write five sentences about your own week using the verbs дать, писать, звонить, помогать, and отвечать, with a different person as recipient each time and at least one plural. Model response for one line: Вчера я помогла брату (vchee-RA ya pa-mag-LA BRA-too) — yesterday I helped my brother, with a feminine past form because the speaker is a woman. Self-review checks four points: the verb's governing case, the noun's declension, the single or plural number, and the absence of an added preposition. Then read the five sentences aloud and underline every dative ending, which converts an abstract label into a visible marking habit. The task is nonblocking and worth repeating after a week.
depth.summary: The dative is the case of the person who receives, benefits, or is affected, and it is written on the noun as -у/-ю, -е, -ии, or -ам/-ям. Because the endings are largely unique to this case in the plural, the plural is where a beginner's dative is heard most clearly. Transfer the habit of asking first which case a verb governs, then which declension the noun belongs to.

lessons.title: Impersonal sentences: Мне холодно, мне нужно, мне нравится
lessons.explanation: Russian often describes a state without naming anyone as subject. Instead of saying I am cold, it says, roughly, to me it is cold: Мне холодно (mnye KHO-lad-na) — I am cold. Мне is the dative pronoun you met in lesson 61, and холодно is a predicative form, a word that behaves like is plus an adjective without ever taking one. The same frame carries a whole family of states: тепло (teep-LO) warm, жарко (ZHAR-ka) hot, скучно (SKOOSH-na) bored, трудно (TROOD-na) hard for me, легко (lyeg-KO) easy for me, интересно (in-tee-RYES-na) interesting to me, ясно (YAS-na) clear to me. Because nothing is the subject, the sentence has no nominative noun and no nominative pronoun. Spanish gives you two very different bridges here. For sensations Spanish says tengo frío, literally I have cold, which makes the person the subject and therefore teaches the wrong reflex; Russian keeps the person in the dative. For liking, Spanish says me gusta la música, and that structure matches Russian almost perfectly: Мне нравится музыка (mnye NRA-veet-sya MOO-zy-ka) — I like music. Where Russian goes further is that the state can be put in the past or the future by adding a form of быть: Мне было холодно (mnye BY-la KHO-lad-na) — I was cold; Мне будет скучно (mnye BOO-det SKOOSH-na) — I will be bored.
lessons.example: Build the frame in three steps with the same person. Step one, a state: Мне холодно (mnye KHO-lad-na) — I am cold. Step two, a need with a thing: Мне нужна ручка (mnye noozh-NA ROOCH-ka) — I need a pen. Here нужна is not a verb but a short-form word that agrees with the thing needed, so the pen's gender chooses the shape. Change the thing and the shape follows: Мне нужно время (mnye NOOZH-na VRYE-mya) — I need time, neuter; Мне нужны билеты (mnye noozh-NY bee-LYE-ty) — I need tickets, plural. Step three, a need with an action: Мне нужно работать (mnye NOOZH-na ra-BO-tat) — I need to work, where the infinitive replaces the thing. Now move the whole frame into the past: Мне была нужна ручка (mnye by-LA noozh-NA ROOCH-ka) — I needed a pen. Read each sentence with the stress marks, then say it at normal speed while asking one question aloud: what word, if any, is in the nominative here? In Мне холодно the answer is none, and in Мне нужна ручка it is ручка.
lessons.question: Why does Мне нравятся эти книги (mnye NRA-vyat-sya EH-tee KNEE-gee) — I like these books take a plural verb, while Мне холодно has no subject to agree with at all?
lessons.answer: Нравиться is a verb whose grammatical subject is the thing liked, so these books, being plural, control the plural ending; холодно is a predicative word in a subjectless sentence, so nothing agrees with anything.
lessons.distractor: The plural ending agrees with мне, because the person is the one doing the liking and therefore the logical subject.
lessons.correction: Agreement never runs from the dative experiencer. In Мне нравятся эти книги the nominative noun книги is the subject and fixes the verb's number and person; мне only says who experiences the liking. In Мне холодно there is no nominative noun at all, which is why Russian grammars call such sentences impersonal and why no agreement question even arises. The two frames look alike because both begin with мне, but they are different machines: one hides a nominative subject behind a dative experiencer, the other has no subject.

depth.definitions: An impersonal sentence is one with no grammatical subject in the nominative. A predicative (Russian grammars also say category of state or o-form) is a word such as холодно, нужно, or скучно that functions as the predicate of such a sentence, carrying the is of English without any verb. The experiencer is the person who feels or needs something; in Russian dative impersonals the experiencer stands in the dative. Agreement is the matching of a verb or short-form word to the number and gender of its nominative subject. These four terms are what the rest of this lesson turns on.
depth.mechanism: The dative frame exists because Russian can express a state without claiming that anyone is its agent. Cold is not something the speaker does; it is a condition that holds of the speaker, and the grammar encodes that by removing the nominative position entirely. Where a thing is needed, a second mechanism appears: short-form нужен, нужна, нужно, нужны agrees with the needed thing rather than with the person, so the sentence contains a nominative subject even though the person remains dative. Wikipedia's account of Russian impersonal sentences classifies these as dative impersonals and notes explicitly that the analysis is disputed, since some scholars treat the dative experiencer as an oblique subject rather than as an object. The teaching consequence is honest and simple: use the construction confidently, but do not treat the label subjectless as a settled theoretical claim. One limit matters for production: an o-form predicate has no agreement slot, so you cannot make it match the person; only the нужен family and ordinary verbs have something to match.
depth.secondExample: Two sentences, two tenses, two different agreement behaviours. Мне было холодно утром (mnye BY-la KHO-lad-na OO-tram) — I was cold in the morning: было is the neuter past of быть used because there is no subject to agree with, and холодно never changes. Теперь мне нужны тёплые ботинки (tee-PYER mnye noozh-NY TYO-ply-ye ba-TEEN-kee) — now I need warm boots: need is now carried by a short form that agrees with ботинки in the plural, and the adjective тёплые agrees with the same noun. Put the two sentences side by side and the contrast is mechanical: in the first, nothing agrees; in the second, two words must agree with the thing rather than with the person.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first makes the person a subject: Я холодно or Я скучно, which a Russian speaker hears as a broken sentence. The second fixes the shape of нужно and ignores the thing: Мне нужно билеты instead of Мне нужны билеты. The third uses a full adjective where a short form or predicative is required: Мне холодный or Мне нужная ручка. The fourth puts the liking in the wrong place: Я нравлюсь книги, which in fact means the books like me, a genuinely confusing sentence to produce. Diagnose in this order: name the person, confirm they are in the dative; name the thing, if there is one, and check that any agreeing word matches it; then check whether the sentence needs a verb at all.
depth.application: Optional practice: write six impersonal sentences about a single day, using at least two o-forms, two нужен-family sentences with different genders, and one past-tense sentence with было. Model response for one line: Утром мне было холодно, а теперь мне нужен горячий чай (OO-tram mnye BY-la KHO-lad-na, a tee-PYER mnye NOO-zhen ga-RYA-chee chai) — in the morning I was cold, and now I need hot tea. Self-review checks four things: the person is dative, the state word is an o-form or short form rather than a full adjective, any agreeing word matches the thing and not the person, and past or future time is carried by было or будет. Read the six sentences aloud and mark each one as subjectless or subject-bearing, which is the single most useful diagnostic in this construction. The task is nonblocking.
depth.summary: Dative impersonals let Russian state a condition without a nominative subject: the person stands in the dative and the state is carried by a predicative o-form, by нужно, or by a short form that agrees with the thing involved. Spanish tengo frío is a false friend in structure, while me gusta is a genuine one. Separate the two machines clearly: one has no subject at all, the other hides a nominative subject behind a dative experiencer.

visual.description: A labelled decision sequence for the dative experiential construction, separating subjectless states from need-and-liking sentences that hide a nominative subject.
steps: Ask what kind of meaning you are expressing: a physical or emotional state, a need for a thing, a need to act, or a liking.
For a state, use an o-form with the person in the dative and build past or future with было or будет; nothing agrees.
For a thing needed, use нужен / нужна / нужно / нужны and make it agree with the thing, not with the person.

For a liking, use нравится or нравятся, and let the thing liked be the nominative subject that fixes the verb's number.
Check the finished sentence for any nominative word, and confirm it is the thing (if any), never the person.

lessons.title: The instrumental for the means: writing with a pen, paying by card
lessons.explanation: Spanish and English both use a small word before the instrument: escribir con un bolígrafo, write with a pen. Russian uses no such word. It changes the ending of the noun instead: Я пишу ручкой (ya pee-SHOO ROOCH-kay) — I write with a pen. The ending -ой on ручкой is the instrumental case, and the instrumental's core job is to name the means by which something is done. The forms are regular. Masculine and neuter nouns take -ом, spelled -ем after a soft stem: нож (nozh) — knife becomes ножом (na-ZHOM); словарь becomes словарём. Feminine -а nouns take -ой, spelled -ей after a soft stem: ручка (ROOCH-ka) — pen becomes ручкой (ROOCH-kay); ложка (LOSH-ka) — spoon becomes ложкой (LOSH-kay). Feminine nouns with a soft-sign ending take -ью: дверь (dvyer) — door becomes дверью. In the plural every gender takes -ами, or -ями after a soft stem: руками (roo-KA-mee) — with hands; деньгами (dyen-GA-mee) — with money. Because no preposition is used, the ending does all the work, and that is exactly why the common error here is to add the Spanish preposition's Russian cousin с: Я пишу с ручкой sounds like writing in the company of a pen. Cornell warns about this directly. The instrumental plural -ами is also easy to confuse with the dative plural -ам you learned in lesson 61, so pay attention to the final sound: друзьям (drooz-YAM) to friends against друзьями (drooz-YA-mee) with friends.
lessons.example: Describe a small domestic task and watch the case do all the work. Я режу хлеб ножом (ya RYE-zhoo khlyeb na-ZHOM) — I cut bread with a knife: хлеб is the thing acted on, accusative; ножом is the instrument, instrumental; no preposition appears. Я ем суп ложкой (ya yem soop LOSH-kay) — I eat soup with a spoon, same pattern with a feminine noun. Я открываю дверь ключом (ya at-kry-VA-yu dvyer klyoo-CHOM) — I open the door with a key. Now change one word to see that the case choice is a choice about meaning, not decoration: Я ем суп со сметаной (ya yem soop sa smee-TA-nay) — I eat soup with sour cream. Sour cream is not the means of eating; it is an addition, so the sentence uses с plus the instrumental. The difference between ложкой and со сметаной is the difference between the tool and the company. Contrast the instrument with a carried object in one more pair: Я пришла с ручкой (ya preesh-LA s ROOCH-kay) — I arrived with a pen, where the pen is something I brought, against Я пишу ручкой, where it is the means. Read the four sentences aloud with the marked stress, then say them at normal speed while asking one question per sentence: is this noun the means, or is it something added?
lessons.question: Why does Я пишу ручкой (ya pee-SHOO ROOCH-kay) need no preposition when Spanish says con un bolígrafo?
lessons.answer: The instrumental ending itself means 'by means of', so the case carries the relation that Spanish puts in the preposition con.
lessons.distractor: Russian drops prepositions before any noun that names a physical object, so no rule is involved.
lessons.correction: The omission is not general: the same noun in an accompaniment sense does take a preposition, as in Я пришла с ручкой (ya preesh-LA s ROOCH-kay) — I arrived with a pen, where the pen is an object I brought, not the means I used. Russian therefore distinguishes instrument from companion by the presence or absence of с, while Spanish leaves both meanings to con. Learn the pair together rather than treating the bare instrumental as a missing preposition.

depth.definitions: The instrumental case marks the means, instrument, or agent through which an action is carried out. It also marks accompaniment when it follows the preposition с, and it marks the role in predicate constructions, which lesson 64 develops. The relevant ending families are -ом/-ем (masculine and neuter singular), -ой/-ей and -ью (feminine singular), and -ами/-ями (all genders in the plural). An instrument is a physical or abstract tool; an accompaniment is something or someone present along with the subject. Distinguishing those two roles is the whole task of this lesson.
depth.mechanism: The reason Russian can express the instrument without a preposition is that its case endings are semantically loaded: the instrumental ending is a small morpheme meaning by means of. Once that morpheme exists, an extra preposition would be redundant for the instrument and is therefore reserved for a different meaning. Cornell's instrumental page states the contrast explicitly, warning that using с where no preposition belongs shifts the meaning to something else entirely, and its companion page shows that the instrumental with с, под, между, and за expresses accompaniment or spatial relations instead. Two limits are worth knowing early. First, not every means of doing something is a physical tool: the same ending covers abstract means such as деньгами with money, so the category is semantic, not physical. Second, the instrumental is not the only way Russian expresses how something is done; adverbs such as пешком on foot do the same job lexically, and lesson 66 meets them again with means of transport.
depth.secondExample: Hold the verb платить (pla-TEET) to pay fixed and vary the means. Я плачу картой (ya pla-CHOO KAR-tay) — I pay by card. Я плачу наличными (ya pla-CHOO na-LEECH-ny-mee) — I pay in cash, an instrumental plural that behaves as a set phrase. Now change to accompaniment and the sentence needs a human: Я плачу за обед (ya pla-CHOO za a-BYED) — I pay for lunch, which is a different prepositional pattern again. The three sentences share a verb and a situation but three different structures, which is precisely why paying vocabulary is worth drilling as whole phrases rather than as isolated words. Note also that картой and наличными are not optional decorations: without the instrumental ending the sentence would have no way to say how the payment happened, since Russian has no equivalent of the English preposition by in this construction.
depth.mistake: Three errors recur. The first transfers Spanish con and writes Я пишу с ручкой, which means writing in the pen's company. The second keeps the dictionary form and writes Я режу хлеб нож, leaving the means unmarked. The third confuses the two plural endings and writes Я пишу друзьям when the friends are companions and друзьями when they are means, or the reverse; the failure is not pronunciation but case identification. Diagnose by asking a single question of each noun in the sentence: is this the thing acted on, the means, or something accompanying me? Only after that answer should you write an ending, and only the means answer takes a bare instrumental.
depth.application: Optional practice: choose five ordinary tasks you did today, such as writing, cutting, opening, paying, and travelling, and write one sentence for each with an instrumental of means; then write two sentences in which the same object appears as an accompaniment with с, and mark the meaning difference in one clause each. Model response for a pair: Я открыла дверь ключом (ya at-KRY-la dvyer klyoo-CHOM) — I opened the door with a key, against Я пришла с ключом (ya preesh-LA s klyoo-CHOM) — I came with the key (in my bag). Self-review checks three things: no preposition before a means, correct ending family for the noun's gender and number, and a clear English gloss that says by means of or with in the tool sense. Read the sentences aloud and underline the instrumental endings. The task is nonblocking.
depth.summary: The instrumental names the means by which an action is done and does so without a preposition, because the ending itself carries the meaning by means of. Adding с changes the role from instrument to accompaniment, which is why the same noun can appear in both shapes with different meanings. Learn the plural pair -ам (recipient) against -ами (means) as a deliberate contrast, and treat task vocabulary such as платить картой as a phrase rather than a word.

lessons.title: Instrumental for company and for roles: с другом, работает врачом
lessons.explanation: Lesson 63 gave the instrumental to the means. The same case has a second large job: naming the company you keep and the role you hold. Company takes the preposition с: Я иду в кино с другом (ya ee-DOO f kee-NO s DROO-gam) — I am going to the cinema with a friend. Я живу с родителями (ya zhee-VOO s ra-DEE-tye-lya-mee) — I live with my parents. Before an awkward cluster, с becomes со: со мной (sa MNOY) with me, со сметаной with sour cream. Roles are expressed by the instrumental with no preposition at all, and this is where English and Spanish lead you astray. Spanish says trabaja como médica; Russian says Она работает врачом (a-NA ra-BO-ta-yet VRA-chom) — she works as a doctor, with no word for as. The verbs that take a role this way are called linking verbs: работать to work, стать to become, быть to be in the past or future, считаться to be considered. Because the role names the same person as the subject, Russian marks that sameness with the instrumental rather than with a separate word. Compare the two present-tense sentences that exist side by side: Она врач (a-NA vrach) — she is a doctor, where there is no verb and both words stand in the nominative, and Она работает врачом, where the role must take the instrumental. Spanish gets you halfway here as well, since ser médico uses a bare noun, but it gives you no signal that Russian's verbless present behaves differently from Russian's verbs of role.
lessons.example: Build the role sentence in three tenses, then add company. Present with a verb: Мой брат работает инженером (moy brat ra-BO-ta-yet in-zhee-NYE-ram) — my brother works as an engineer. Present without a verb: Мой брат инженер (moy brat in-zhee-NYER) — my brother is an engineer, with no instrumental because there is no verb to govern it. Past: Раньше он был инженером (RAN-she on byl in-zhee-NYE-ram) — he used to be an engineer. Future or intention: Он хочет стать инженером (on KHO-chet stat in-zhee-NYE-ram) — he wants to become an engineer. Now add company to the same family scene: Вчера я была в театре с сестрой (vchee-RA ya by-LA f tee-A-trye s sees-TROY) — yesterday I was at the theatre with my sister. The penultimate and final sentences both end in an instrumental, but one marks a role and the other a companion; only the preposition tells them apart. Read the five sentences with the stress marks, then at normal speed, saying the label role or company after each noun.
lessons.question: What is the difference between Она врач (a-NA vrach) and Она работает врачом (a-NA ra-BO-ta-yet VRA-chom), and why does only one of them contain an instrumental?
lessons.answer: They describe the same role; the verbless present equates subject and role with two nominative words, while работать is a linking verb that governs the instrumental for the role.
lessons.distractor: Она врач describes a permanent situation and Она работает врачом a temporary one, and Russian marks the difference with the case.
lessons.correction: Nothing in the two sentences concerns permanence. Russian expresses am/is/are with no verb at all in the present, and a linking verb such as работать, стать, or быть takes the instrumental because the role word names the same person as the subject. So the presence of the instrumental is a consequence of the verb, not of how long the job lasts. The same contrast appears in the past: Он врач now, Он был врачом before, with the instrumental appearing only once быть enters the sentence.

depth.definitions: A linking verb joins two words that refer to the same entity, as in John became a doctor, where John and doctor name one person. The instrumental case marks the second name in such constructions, and it also marks accompaniment when introduced by с. Accompaniment means being present together with someone or something; a role predicate means being identified as something. с plus the genitive is a different construction entirely, meaning from or off, as in упала со стола. Finally, the preposition со is simply the form с takes before clusters that begin with с, з, ш, ж, or мн.
depth.mechanism: The predicate instrumental exists because Russian needs a way to show that a noun is a second designation of the subject rather than a separate entity. If the role were simply another accusative object, Он работает врачом would be indistinguishable in shape from Он видит врача, and the language would lose the sameness that linking verbs assert. Cornell's page on linking verbs notes honestly that the category is vague and that even работать counts as a linking verb only when it is synonymous with быть, and it adds the important practical point that a good dictionary, not intuition, settles which case a given verb wants. Extension at the edge of the pattern: some verbs take two objects with a linking relationship, and there the first stands in the accusative and the second in the instrumental, as in Сашу выбрали председателем (SA-shoo VY-bra-lee pree-see-DA-tye-lyem) — they elected Sasha chairman. The pattern is productive but not unlimited, which is why the dictionary caveat matters.
depth.secondExample: Two minimal pairs keep the two jobs apart. First, company against origin: Я гуляла с братом (ya goo-LYA-la s BRA-tam) — I was walking with my brother, companion, instrumental; Я вернулась с работы (ya vyer-NOO-las s ra-BO-ty) — I came back from work, origin, genitive. Second, role in the present against role in the past: Сейчас она врач (see-CHAAS a-NA vrach) — she is a doctor now; Десять лет назад она была врачом (DYE-syat lyet na-ZAD a-NA by-LA VRA-chom) — ten years ago she was a doctor. The change of case across time in the second pair is caused entirely by the arrival of был, and the change of case across the first pair is caused entirely by the meaning of с. Nothing about the nouns themselves changed.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first uses the instrument only and forgets the companion preposition: Я иду в кино другом. The second adds the preposition where a role is meant: Она работает с врачом means she works alongside a doctor, not that she is one, so the missing preposition is meaningful. The third imports Spanish como or English as and writes Она работает как врач, which is not the Russian construction. The fourth drops работать or стать altogether and writes Он врачом without a verb to govern the case. Diagnose by locating the verb first: if the verb is работать, стать, быть, or считаться, the role word is instrumental; if there is no verb, the role word is nominative.
depth.application: Optional practice: write five sentences about the occupations and family roles of people you know, using работать plus instrumental in at least two, a verbless present in one, and был or была in one; then add three sentences about whom you did things with this week, using с plus instrumental. Model response for one line: Моя сестра работает учительницей (ma-YA sees-TRA ra-BO-ta-yet oo-chee-TYEL-nee-tsay) — my sister works as a teacher, feminine instrumental in -ей after a soft stem. Self-review checks four things: the verb is a linking verb or absent, the role ending matches gender and number, the companion sentences keep с, and the с-plus-genitive meaning from or off was not confused with с plus instrumental. Read the eight sentences aloud and mark each instrumental as role or company. The task is nonblocking.
depth.summary: The instrumental carries two distinct jobs beyond the means: company, introduced by с, and role, governed by linking verbs such as работать, стать, быть, and считаться. The preposition is the whole difference between с другом with a friend and работает врачом works as a doctor, so it must never be added or dropped carelessly. When in doubt about which case a verb wants, the dictionary is the authority, and Russian's verbless present is the one place where no instrumental appears at all.

lessons.title: One transaction, four roles: reading a real exchange
lessons.explanation: You now own four role markers: the accusative for the thing acted on, the dative for the recipient, the instrumental without a preposition for the means, and the instrumental with с for company. Real sentences use several at once, so the skill this lesson builds is not another ending but a routine for reading a whole exchange. Take a short shopping scene. — Что ты ищешь? (shto ty EE-shchesh) — what are you looking for? — Я ищу подарок маме (ya ee-SHCHOO pa-DA-rak MA-mye) — I am looking for a gift for mum. The answer contains two roles in three words: подарок is the thing, accusative and unchanged in shape because it is an inanimate masculine noun; маме is a recipient in the dative, and it needs no preposition. The conversation continues: — А платить картой? (a pla-TEET KAR-tay) — and are you paying by card? — Да, картой — yes, by card: a bare instrumental of means. Put the whole thing in one narrated sentence: Вчера я купила маме подарок и заплатила картой (vchee-RA ya koo-PEE-la MA-mye pa-DA-rak ee za-pla-TEE-la KAR-tay) — yesterday I bought mum a gift and paid by card. Spanish would say le compré un regalo a mi mamá y pagué con tarjeta, spreading the same information across le, a, and con; Russian carries all of it inside two noun endings and one verb ending. Russian also allows the recipient to move for emphasis, so Маме я купила подарок is a legitimate variant, which means word order is not a reliable clue and the endings must be read first.
lessons.example: Read a second transaction the same way, one role at a time. Scene: you show friends photographs, and you took them with your phone. Я показала друзьям фотографии (ya pa-ka-ZA-la drooz-YAM fa-ta-GRA-fee-ee) — I showed my friends the photographs: друзьям is a dative plural recipient in -ям, фотографии is an accusative plural thing. Я сняла их телефоном (ya SNEE-la eekh tee-lye-FO-nam) — I took them with my phone: их is the accusative object pronoun, телефоном is a bare instrumental of means; there is no preposition and none is needed. Now add company and a place: Вчера я ходила в парк с братом (vchee-RA ya kha-DEE-la f park s BRA-tam) — yesterday I went to the park with my brother, where в парк is direction, accusative, and с братом is company, instrumental. Four sentences, six case decisions. Before each ending, say the role out loud: recipient, thing, means, company, direction. Only then write or read the ending, and only then check whether a preposition is present or absent.
lessons.question: In Я купила маме подарок и заплатила картой, which noun is dative and which is instrumental, and what does each role mean?
lessons.answer: Маме is dative and marks the recipient or beneficiary, while картой is instrumental and marks the means of payment; neither noun takes a preposition.
lessons.distractor: Маме is dative and marks the means of payment, while картой is instrumental and marks the person who benefits.
lessons.correction: The roles are fixed by the verbs, not by the nouns' shapes. Купить in this pattern places the person in the dative as beneficiary and the thing in the accusative, while платить takes a bare instrumental for the means of payment, which is also why paying vocabulary is learned as whole phrases. Reversing the two roles produces a sentence in which mum is the means of payment, which is nonsense but grammatically well formed, and that is exactly why the roles, not the endings, must be decided first.

depth.definitions: A role in this lesson means the semantic part a noun plays in the clause: recipient, thing acted on, means, companion, or direction. Russian marks roles with case endings and, for some roles, with prepositions attached to particular verbs, a property grammars call government. Government is a property of the verb, so купить and платить differ not in meaning alone but in the bare or prepositional shapes they require. Word order in Russian carries emphasis and information structure rather than grammatical role, which is the assumption that makes the labelling routine necessary.
depth.mechanism: The whole system works because Russian splits role marking between endings and prepositions, while Spanish and English lean on small words and position. Once you notice that, the reading routine becomes mechanical: identify the verb, list the roles it needs, assign each noun to a role, then write the case that role requires, adding a preposition only where a specific verb requires one. Cornell's pages on prepositions make this concrete, showing verbs whose government pattern fixes a particular preposition and case, such as перевести на plus accusative for translate into, играть в plus accusative for play a game, and попросить у plus genitive for request from somebody. The limitation to state plainly is that no general rule predicts an individual verb's government pattern, and Russian dictionaries record it entry by entry, so a beginner should treat each new verb as carrying a small note about the cases it wants. Word order adds one more caution: because emphasis can move the recipient to the front, a sentence's first noun is not automatically its subject, and the endings remain the reliable evidence.
depth.secondExample: A work message using three roles at once: Скажи, пожалуйста, директору, что я отправила ему отчёт утром (ska-ZHEE pa-ZHA-loos-ta dee-RYEK-ta-roo, shto ya at-PRA-vee-la ye-MOO at-CHYOT OO-tram) — please tell the director that I sent him the report in the morning. Директору is a dative recipient governed by сказать; ему is the dative pronoun for the same person as the indirect object of отправить; отчёт is the accusative thing sent. Nothing here needs a preposition, and nothing here depends on position: the time phrase could equally stand first, as Утром я отправила директору отчёт, and every case ending would stay exactly as it is. That stability is the point to notice. Moving words in Russian changes emphasis and information structure; it never changes which noun is the recipient and which is the thing, because the endings carry that information independently of order.
depth.mistake: Three errors recur once several roles appear together. The first assigns cases by position and treats the first noun as the recipient or the last noun as the thing, which fails the moment a speaker reorders for emphasis. The second adds a preposition because Spanish would: пишу к маме for a plain recipient, or плачу с картой for a means. The third collapses the two instrumentals into one and writes с другом for a means, which turns an instrument into company. Diagnose by writing the roles in a column before the endings, then checking two things only: does the role normally take a preposition, and does the verb's entry say otherwise? If the roles are correct and the endings are wrong, the gap is form retrieval; if the roles are wrong, the gap is the labelling routine itself, and that is the higher-priority repair.
depth.application: Optional practice: take one real five-line exchange from your week, such as arranging where to meet or buying something, and write it out in Russian with a role label above every noun. Then produce a single narrated sentence that reports the exchange using at least one dative recipient, one instrumental of means, and one accusative thing. Model response: Сегодня я звонила сестре, и мы вместе купили билеты в театр; я заплатила картой (see-VOD-nya ya zva-NEE-la sees-TRYE, ee my VMYE-stye koo-PEE-lee bee-LYE-ty f tee-ATR; ya za-pla-TEE-la KAR-tay) — today I phoned my sister, and together we bought theatre tickets; I paid by card. Self-review checks four things: every noun has a role label, every ending matches the role and the noun's declension, prepositions appear only where the verb requires one, and the English gloss accounts for every ending rather than silently dropping one. The task is nonblocking and is the natural preparation for the unit quiz.
depth.summary: Real Russian distributes meaning across endings and prepositions while leaving word order free for emphasis. The reliable routine is to name each noun's role, retrieve the case that role requires, and add a preposition only when the verb's own entry requires one. Spanish gives you useful role intuitions through le and a, but it also tempts you to add prepositions where Russian has none, so the presence or absence of a preposition is a fact to verify, not to guess.

questions.prompt: A learner wants to say 'I answered my sister' and writes Я ответила сестру. Diagnose the error and name what the verb actually requires.
questions.answer: The person must stand in the dative: Я ответила сестре, because отвечать governs the dative for the person answered, with no preposition.
questions.distractor: The noun is right but the aspect is wrong, because ответить is perfective and therefore cannot describe a single completed answer.
questions.correction: The error is one of case government, not aspect: ответить is the natural perfective for a single completed act, and the sentence is fine once the person takes the dative ending -е. The accusative сестру would make the sister the thing answered rather than the person addressed. Cornell's verb list for the dative names отвечать among the verbs that place the person in this case, which is why the repair is a change of ending rather than of verb.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence Мне ___ эти фотографии, meaning that you like them, and state which word determines the form you chose.
questions.answer: нравятся, because эти фотографии is the nominative subject and a plural subject forces the plural verb form, while мне only names the person who experiences the liking.
questions.distractor: нравится, because impersonal sentences always keep the verb in a fixed singular form regardless of the nouns around it.
questions.correction: The fixed-singular assumption is true of the o-form type such as Мне холодно, which has no subject at all, but false for нравиться, which is an ordinary verb with a nominative subject. Distinguish the two machines before choosing a form: check whether any noun in the sentence could be its subject, and if one can, the verb must agree with it.

questions.prompt: At the till a learner says Я плачу с картой. What has gone wrong, and what should the sentence be?
questions.answer: The card is the means of payment, so it takes a bare instrumental with no preposition: Я плачу картой.
questions.distractor: The card should stand in the genitive after с, giving Я плачу с карты, because с always requires the genitive case.
questions.correction: The preposition с does not always take the genitive: с plus the instrumental marks company, while с plus the genitive marks origin or separation, as in книга упала со стола. Since a card here is the means rather than a companion, no preposition belongs in the sentence at all, and that absence is exactly what makes the meaning unambiguous.

questions.prompt: A friend has just qualified and now works as a nurse. Write the Russian sentence and explain the case of the role word; then say what changes if the verb is dropped.
questions.answer: Она работает медсестрой, with the role in the instrumental because работать is a linking verb; without a verb the present-tense equation reads Она медсестра, with two nominative words and no instrumental.
questions.distractor: Она работает медсестра, because Russian keeps the nominative for a role whenever the same person is the subject of the sentence.
questions.correction: The nominative role word belongs only to the verbless present, where nothing governs a case. As soon as a linking verb such as работать, стать, быть, or считаться appears, the role word is governed in the instrumental. Notice too that Spanish trabaja como enfermera invites you to insert a word for as, and Russian has none.

questions.prompt: Report one day in a single sentence: yesterday you wrote to your mother and sent her photographs using your phone. Identify each noun's role and case.
questions.answer: Вчера я написала маме и отправила ей фотографии телефоном, where маме and ей are dative recipients, фотографии is the accusative thing sent, and телефоном is a bare instrumental of means.
questions.distractor: Вчера я написала маму и отправила её фотографии с телефоном, where the recipient is accusative and the means is expressed with с plus the instrumental.
questions.correction: Писать and отправить both take the person in the dative, and the pronoun ей substitutes for маме without changing the case. Фотографии is plural accusative and stays accusative because it is inanimate. The means of sending takes the bare instrumental, which is why телефоном has no preposition; adding с would turn the phone into an object accompanying you rather than the instrument of the action.

lessons.title: Going and going regularly: идти and ходить, ехать and ездить
lessons.explanation: Russian has no single verb for go. It has pairs whose members differ in how the motion is shaped, not in how far it goes. Идти (eet-TEE) describes motion on foot in one direction, in progress, right now: Сейчас я иду в библиотеку (see-CHAAS ya ee-DOO v beeb-lee-a-TYE-koo) — right now I am walking to the library. Ходить (kha-DEET) describes the same on-foot motion when it is habitual, round-trip, or directionless: Я хожу в библиотеку каждый день (ya kha-ZHOO v beeb-lee-a-TYE-koo KAZH-dy dyen) — I go to the library every day. The pair for motion by vehicle is ехать (YE-khat) and ездить (YEZ-deet): Я еду в Москву (ya YE-doo v mask-VOO) — I am travelling to Moscow; Я езжу в Москву каждый год (ya YEZ-zhoo v mask-VOO KAZH-dy got) — I go to Moscow every year. The choice depends on the kind of motion, never on the distance: a two-minute walk across a room still uses идти, and a two-hour drive still uses ехать. Two further forms make the system usable. Пойти and поехать are perfective and mean set out or take off, used for a plan: Завтра я поеду в Москву (ZAF-tra ya pa-YE-doo v mask-VOO) — tomorrow I will travel to Moscow. Сходить and съездить are perfective and mean the motion has been completed and returned from: Я сходила в аптеку (ya skha-DEE-la v ap-TYE-koo) — I went to the pharmacy and came back. Spanish has nothing like this split, since voy covers both standing there and going regularly, so the learner must consciously decide which shape of motion is meant before choosing a verb.
lessons.example: Contrast one day against one habit with the same destination. Yesterday, one completed trip: Вчера я ходила в кино (vchee-RA ya kha-DEE-la f kee-NO) — yesterday I went to the cinema, round trip, so the multi-directional verb is used. In the middle of that same trip: Когда я шла в кино, я встретила друга (kag-DA ya shla f kee-NO, ya FSTRYE-tee-la DROO-ga) — while I was walking to the cinema I met a friend, one-directional motion in progress, so идти appears in its past form шла, feminine because the speaker is a woman. Now a habit: Я хожу в кино каждую субботу (ya kha-ZHOO f kee-NO KAZH-doo-yoo soo-BO-too) — I go to the cinema every Saturday. And a plan: Завтра я пойду в кино (ZAF-tra ya pay-DOO f kee-NO) — tomorrow I will go to the cinema, where пойду is a perfective non-past form, which is how Russian builds a future for motion. Read the four sentences aloud, marking each one aloud as one-way, round-trip, habit, or plan before you say it, because the label is what selects the verb.
lessons.question: A learner writes Каждый день я иду в библиотеку for I go to the library every day. What is wrong, and why?
lessons.answer: The repeated round trip requires the multi-directional verb: Каждый день я хожу в библиотеку, because идти describes one-directional motion in progress.
lessons.distractor: Nothing is wrong with the verb; the error is the preposition, since в should be на with the word библиотека.
lessons.correction: The preposition в is correct: библиотека is an ordinary enclosed place, so в plus the accusative marks the destination. The failure is the verb's shape. Идти reports motion happening in one direction at one moment, so it cannot describe a daily routine; ходить reports the motion as a habit or as a completed round trip. The test is not distance or frequency words alone but the shape of the motion: if you are on the way now, use идти; if you go and come back as a matter of habit, use ходить.

depth.definitions: Verbs of motion form pairs whose members are traditionally labelled one-way (also determinate) and non-one-way (also multidirectional or indeterminate). Идти and ехать are one-way; ходить and ездить are non-one-way. Aspect is a separate axis: all four unprefixed verbs are imperfective, while пойти, поехать, сходить, and съездить are perfective. Means of conveyance selects the root, not the prefix: on foot versus by vehicle. Directionality, aspect, and conveyance are three independent choices, and every motion sentence involves all three.
depth.mechanism: The pair exists because Russian encodes the shape of an event rather than only its occurrence. Wikipedia's account of Russian verbs of motion describes Russian as a satellite-framed language, in which the manner of motion is carried by the verb root and the path by prefixes, and it lists the standard pairs including идти and ходить, ехать and ездить, лететь and летать. That framing explains why the same root recurs with different prefixes: the root supplies the kind of movement and the prefix supplies the route through space, a division of labour lesson 67 uses directly. Three limits deserve emphasis. First, English and Spanish do not require you to state this distinction, so translating your intended English sentence will not reveal which verb Russian wants; you must decide the shape first. Second, the non-one-way verb is the normal choice for a completed round trip, which is why Я ходила в кино means I went and came back, while Я шла в кино only reports being on the way. Third, a handful of verbs of motion behave idiomatically, as in идёт дождь for rain is falling, so the pattern is productive rather than exceptionless.
depth.secondExample: Use the same habit frame to choose between walking and riding, and between habit and plan. Habit on foot: Я хожу на работу пешком (ya kha-ZHOO na ra-BO-too pyesh-KOM) — I walk to work, on foot, where пешком is the adverb on foot and no verb root for riding appears. Habit by vehicle: Я езжу на работу на метро (ya YEZ-zhoo na ra-BO-too na meet-RO) — I go to work by metro, where на plus the prepositional names the vehicle. Plan: Завтра я поеду на работу на автобусе (ZAF-tra ya pa-YE-doo na ra-BO-too na af-TO-boo-sye) — tomorrow I will go to work by bus. Notice that the phrase for by a vehicle stays на plus the prepositional in all three sentences, while the verb changes with the shape of the motion. The one phrase that never changes is пешком, which is not a vehicle at all and belongs to the on-foot root.
depth.mistake: Three errors recur. The first uses идти for a habit, producing Каждый день я иду в библиотеку. The second uses ходить while standing in the middle of a journey, so that Я хожу в магазин cannot describe what you are doing right now; only Я иду в магазин can. The third mixes roots and conveyance and produces Я езжу пешком or Я хожу на машине, which contradict themselves. Diagnose by answering three questions in order: is the motion in progress in one direction, or habitual and round-trip, or a plan, or a completed trip; is the mover on foot or in a vehicle; and is the means of transport named with на plus the prepositional. Only then choose the verb.
depth.application: Optional practice: write six sentences about your own movement through a normal week, using both one-way and non-one-way verbs, one perfective plan form, one round-trip form, at least one vehicle phrase with на plus the prepositional, and the adverb пешком once. Model response for a pair: Обычно я хожу в магазин пешком, но вчера я ехала туда на автобусе (a-BYCH-na ya kha-ZHOO v ma-ga-ZEEN pyesh-KOM, no vchee-RA ya YE-kha-la too-DA na af-TO-boo-sye) — usually I walk to the shop, but yesterday I was riding there by bus: the first verb is habitual on foot, the second reports motion by vehicle in progress, and the feminine past form marks the speaker as a woman. Self-review checks four things: the shape of the motion matches the verb, the conveyance matches the root, vehicle phrases use на plus the prepositional, and any perfective form is glossed as a plan or a completed trip rather than as a general habit. The task is nonblocking.
depth.summary: Russian asks which shape the motion has before asking which verb to use: one-way in progress, habitual or round-trip, a plan, or a completed trip. Идти and ходить pair for the feet, ехать and ездить for vehicles, and the perfectives пойти, поехать, сходить, and съездить handle setting out and returning. Spanish voy conceals the contrast, so decide the shape first and let the verb follow.

lessons.title: Prefixes give the path: прийти, уйти, выйти, дойти
lessons.explanation: Lesson 66 gave you roots that say how you move: идти on foot, ехать by vehicle. This lesson adds prefixes, which say which way through space you move. The pattern is regular: a prefix plus the one-way root produces a perfective verb, and its imperfective partner is the same prefix plus the non-one-way root. So войти (vay-TEE) / входить (vkha-DEET) pair for entering, выйти (VY-tee) / выходить (vy-kha-DEET) for exiting, прийти (preet-TEE) / приходить (pree-kha-DEET) for arriving, уйти (oo-TEE) / уходить (oo-kha-DEET) for leaving, and до- adds reaching as far as a point: дойти (day-TEE) to get as far as. The meanings of the common prefixes are worth learning as a set: в- or во- in; вы- out; при- hither, arriving; у- away, leaving; от- away from, especially when carrying something; до- as far as; пере- across; под- up to; за- dropping in; про- past or through. The vehicle roots behave the same way with one adjustment: the imperfective partners are built with -езжать, giving въехать (v-YE-khat) against въезжать (v-yez-ZHAT), приехать (pree-YE-khat) against приезжать (pree-yez-ZHAT), and уехать (oo-YE-khat) against уезжать (oo-yez-ZHAT). The direction cases become systematic too: куда asks where to and takes the accusative, as in в магазин; откуда asks where from and takes the genitive, as in из магазина or с работы; где asks where at and takes the prepositional, as in в магазине. Spanish solves the same problem with separate verbs such as entrar, salir, llegar, irse, and volver, which is easier at first because they are memorised individually, and harder later because Spanish offers no pattern to extend. Russian offers one pattern you can apply to a whole family of meanings.
lessons.example: Use four prefixes with the verb идти and let each one change both the path and the tense machinery. Утром я вышла из дома в восемь (OO-tram ya VYSH-la eez DO-ma v VO-syem) — in the morning I left the house at eight: вы- gives exiting, and из plus the genitive gives the place left. Потом я пришла на работу в девять (pa-TOM ya preesh-LA na ra-BO-too v DYE-vyat) — then I arrived at work at nine: при- gives arriving, and на plus the accusative gives the destination. Вечером я зашла к подруге (VYE-chye-ram ya zash-LA k pad-ROO-gye) — in the evening I dropped in at a friend's place: за- gives a brief stop, and к plus the dative names the person visited. Домой я дошла пешком (da-MOY ya dash-LA pyesh-KOM) — I got home on foot: до- gives reaching as far as, and the distance is implied as completed. And a promise for later: Я зайду к тебе (ya zay-DOO k tee-BYE) — I will drop in at your place, where за- with к plus the dative names the person visited rather than the place entered. Read the four sentences with the stress marks, then say them at normal speed, naming the prefix's direction aloud each time: out, in, aside, as far as. Notice that all four verbs are past-tense perfectives formed from the one-way root; when you want a present-tense or habitual sentence, you switch to прихожу, выхожу, захожу, дохожу.
lessons.question: A learner asks Как дойти до метро? (kak day-TEE da meet-RO) — how do I get to the metro? Why дойти with до rather than войти with в?
lessons.answer: До- means to reach as far as, and it takes до plus the genitive; asking for directions is asking how to reach a place, not how to enter it.
lessons.distractor: Войти cannot be used with метро because метро is an indeclinable noun and therefore cannot take a case ending after в.
lessons.correction: Indeclinable nouns do keep one shape in every case, but that is not why войти is wrong here. Войти means to go into an enclosed space, and it is the natural verb after you are already standing at the entrance; дойти means to get as far as a point, which is exactly what a person asking for directions wants to know. Choose by the path you are describing, not by the noun's declension. Cornell shows the same point in its directions phrase Дойдите до второго светофора.

depth.definitions: A prefix is a small morpheme attached before a root that adds a path or direction meaning. The one-way root is the determinate member of a motion pair, and a prefix on it yields a perfective verb; the non-one-way root with the same prefix yields the imperfective partner. Куда, откуда, and где are the three direction questions, answered with the accusative, the genitive, and the prepositional respectively. The verbs входить, приходить, уходить, выходить, and доходить are the imperfective partners of the prefixed perfectives used above.
depth.mechanism: The reason the pattern works so consistently is that Russian divides the labour cleanly: the root carries the manner of movement and the prefix carries the path. Cornell states the pairing rule plainly, that a one-way verb with a prefix is perfective while its imperfective partner is the prefixed non-one-way verb, and it records the single systematic exception, namely that ехать and ездить build their imperfectives with -езжать. Two limits should be kept in view. First, the meanings of prefixes are tendencies rather than one-to-one labels: у- and от- both express motion away, but the sources distinguish them by whether the speaker's interest lies in the destination or in the absence from the origin, and вы- is used when a closed space is left. That nuance is real but fine-grained, and where textbooks differ the dictionary is the arbiter. Second, the perfective partner cannot carry present meaning: прихожу means I arrive habitually or I am on my way in, while приду or пришла report specific completed events.
depth.secondExample: Follow one person through a doorway and out again, watching the case of the noun change with the path. Она вышла из дома (a-NA VYSH-la eez DO-ma) — she left the house: из plus the genitive, because the house is the source. Она вошла в дом (a-NA vash-LA v dom) — she went into the house: в plus the accusative, because the house is the destination. Она прошла через парк (a-NA prash-LA CHYE-ryez park) — she walked across the park: про- with через plus the accusative expresses passing through. Сейчас она в доме (see-CHAAS a-NA v DO-mye) — she is in the house now: в plus the prepositional, because this is location rather than motion. Four sentences, one person, and the endings alone tell you whether she is moving out of, moving towards, passing through, or simply there.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first uses the wrong root with a prefix, producing въехать for a motion on foot; the prefix is right and the root's manner is wrong. The second carries a prefix onto an imperfective present and produces present-tense perfectives such as я пришёл every day instead of я прихожу каждый день. The third mixes the direction cases, writing из магазин or в магазина. The fourth translates Spanish verbs one by one and loses the shared pattern, so each new sentence must be memorised separately instead of reusing при-, у-, вы-, and до-. Diagnose by naming the path first in plain words, going in, coming out, arriving, leaving, dropping in, getting as far as, then choosing the prefix, then switching roots for aspect only if you need a non-perfective form.
depth.application: Optional practice: narrate one journey in five perfective sentences, then rewrite the same journey as a habitual routine in the present using the imperfective partners. Model response for the first pair: Вчера я вышла из дома, пришла в университет и зашла к деканату (…) — against Каждый день я выхожу из дома, прихожу в университет и захожу в библиотеку (…) — yesterday I left home, arrived at the university, and dropped in at the dean's office, against every day I leave home, arrive at the university, and stop by the library. Self-review checks four things: the prefix matches the path described, the perfective forms are used only for single completed events, the direction case matches the question the phrase answers, and vehicle motion uses the -езжать imperfective rather than a mixed form. The task is nonblocking.
depth.summary: Prefixes turn one root into a family of path meanings: в-, вы-, при-, у-, от-, до-, пере-, под-, за-, and про-. A prefixed one-way verb is perfective and its imperfective partner is the prefixed non-one-way verb, with ехать and ездить forming their partners in -езжать. Direction is also coded in the case after the preposition: accusative for where to, genitive for where from, prepositional for where at.

lessons.title: Where things are and how they get there: стоять, лежать, сидеть
lessons.explanation: English and Spanish both use a single verb for being in a place: is on the table, está en la mesa. Russian chooses among three. Стоять (sta-YAT) means to be standing, лежать (lye-ZHAT) means to be lying, and сидеть (see-DYET) means to be sitting. Only people and animals sit, so сидеть is never used of objects; objects either stand or lie. The choice between the first two follows a rule of thumb that is worth memorising because it is genuinely reliable: an object with a natural base stands, and everything else lies. A glass has a base, so it stands; a plate has a rim that serves as a base, so it stands; a chair has legs, so it stands. A pen, a book lying flat, a key, a map, and a jacket all lie. Compare two statements about the same surface: Стакан стоит на столе (sta-KAN sta-EET na sta-LYE) — the glass is on the table, against Ручка лежит на столе (ROOCH-ka lye-ZHEET na sta-LYE) — the pen is on the table. Alongside the position verbs there is a second family for changing position, arranged in aspect pairs: вставать and встать to get up, ложиться and лечь to lie down or go to bed, садиться and сесть to sit down, ставить and поставить to put something upright, класть and положить to put something down flat. Spanish gives you a partial bridge here, since sentarse, levantarse, and acostarse map cleanly onto садиться, вставать, and ложиться, but estar gives you no help with the stand-or-lie choice, which is the part Russian speakers notice immediately when a learner gets it wrong.
lessons.example: Place three objects in one room and watch the verbs divide the work. На столе стоит чашка (na sta-LYE sta-EET CHASH-ka) — there is a cup on the table: a cup has a base, so it stands. На столе лежит книга (na sta-LYE lye-ZHEET KNEE-ga) — there is a book on the table: a book lies. На диване сидит кошка (na dee-VA-nye see-DEET KOSH-ka) — a cat is sitting on the sofa: сидеть for a living creature. Now change the state and change the aspect: Вчера книга лежала на столе, а сегодня я положила её на полку (vchee-RA KNEE-ga lye-ZHA-la na sta-LYE, a see-VOD-nya ya pa-la-ZHY-la yeyo na POL-koo) — yesterday the book was lying on the table, and today I put it on the shelf. The imperfective лежала describes the unchanging state; the perfective положила reports the completed change. Read the sentences with the stress marks, then at normal speed, and say aloud for each one whether you are describing a state or a change, because that label decides the aspect before the vocabulary is even chosen.
lessons.question: A glass, a pen, and a chair are in a room. Which of стоять, лежать, and сидеть belongs to each, and on what principle?
lessons.answer: Стакан стоит, ручка лежит, стул стоит: standing belongs to objects with a natural base such as a glass or a chair's legs, lying to everything else, and сидеть is reserved for people and animals.
lessons.distractor: All three lie, because лежать is the general verb for an object occupying a position and the other two are stylistic variants.
lessons.correction: Лежать is not a general positional verb; it is the default for objects without a base, and the division between it and стоять is a genuine grammatical choice that native speakers apply automatically. Сидеть would be wrong for the chair because only living beings sit, even though the English sentence says the chair is standing in the corner. The diagnostic is one question: does this object normally rest on a base, such as a bottom, a rim, or legs? If yes, стоять; if no, лежать; if it is alive, сидеть.

depth.definitions: Verbs of position (стоять, лежать, сидеть) are imperfective and describe a state rather than an event. Verbs of putting and getting (ставить/поставить, класть/положить, садиться/сесть, ложиться/лечь, вставать/встать) are aspect pairs whose perfective member reports a completed change of position. Location answers the question где and takes в or на plus the prepositional case; motion answers куда and takes в or на plus the accusative. A natural base is the surface an object normally rests on, such as the bottom of a glass, the rim of a plate, or the legs of a chair.
depth.mechanism: The three-way split exists because Russian treats position as a property of the object rather than purely of the geometry. Cornell states the division plainly: сидеть is never said about objects, and there is a fairly strict distinction between objects that can only stand and those that can only lie, with the base as the practical test. The same page links the position verbs to a second decision, aspect: the imperfective reports the state and the perfective reports the change that produced it, so книга лежала and я положила describe two halves of one story. A further subtlety in the sources is worth recording because it is a genuine limit on the rule of thumb: most change-of-position sentences treat the destination as a point and take the accusative, as in Он сел на стул, but when the destination is a large area rather than a piece of furniture, the prepositional can appear instead, as in Он лёг в гостиной for he lay down in the living room. The sources note that this happens mainly with rooms and other large spaces, so the accusative remains the safe default for chairs and sofas.
depth.secondExample: Run one object through a whole day to see state, place, and change interact. Утром книга лежала на столе (OO-tram KNEE-ga lye-ZHA-la na sta-LYE) — in the morning the book was lying on the table: state, imperfective, location in the prepositional. Днём я взяла книгу и положила её в сумку (dnyom ya vzYa-la KNEE-goo ee pa-la-ZHY-la yeyo f SOOM-koo) — during the day I took the book and put it in the bag: two perfective changes, with the destination в сумку in the accusative. Вечером книга лежала в сумке (VYE-chye-ram KNEE-ga lye-ZHA-la f SOOM-kye) — in the evening the book was lying in the bag: back to the state, with the location in the prepositional. Nothing about the book changed except its position, and the case of сумка shifts from accusative to prepositional as the sentence moves from motion to location.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first uses one verb for everything, usually лежать, as in Стакан лежит на столе. The second applies сидеть to objects, as in Стул сидит у окна. The third keeps the prepositional after a put-verb and writes Я положила ручку на столе, where the destination requires the accusative. The fourth mixes the two families, choosing a change verb to report a state, as in Ручка положила на столе, instead of the state verb Ручка лежит. Diagnose in two steps: for the base test, ask whether the object rests on a bottom, rim, or legs; for aspect and case, ask whether the sentence reports a state or a change and whether the phrase answers где or куда.
depth.application: Optional practice: walk through one room and write six sentences about what is where, using all three position verbs at least once; then write three sentences reporting how three objects got there, using the perfective put-verbs with the accusative of destination. Model response for one pair: На полке стоит ваза, а на столе лежат ключи; Утром я поставила вазу на полку (na POL-kye sta-EET VA-za, a na sta-LYE lye-ZHAT klyoo-CHEE; OO-tram ya pa-STA-vee-la VA-zoo na POL-koo) — a vase stands on the shelf and the keys lie on the table; in the morning I put the vase on the shelf. Self-review checks four things: the position verb matches the object's base and animacy, states are imperfective and changes perfective, locations use the prepositional and destinations the accusative, and the destination phrase uses в or на plus the correct noun form. The task is nonblocking.
depth.summary: Russian splits being in a place into standing, lying, and sitting, with the natural base of an object deciding between the first two and animacy reserving the third for living beings. Position verbs are imperfective states and their aspect partners report completed changes of position. The case follows the meaning: где with the prepositional for where something is, куда with the accusative for where it goes.

lessons.title: Commands, requests, and obligation: садитесь, сядьте, вы должны
lessons.explanation: Russian builds commands from the non-past stem with one of three endings. Add -и when the ending is stressed or the stem ends in a consonant cluster: говори (ga-va-REE) speak, скажи (ska-ZHEE) say. Add -ь when the ending is unstressed and the stem ends in a single consonant: поставь (pa-STAF) put, будь (boot) be. Add -й when the stem ends in a vowel: читай (chee-TAY) read, работай (ra-BO-tay) work. For one person in a polite or plural situation, add -те, giving Читайте (chee-TAY-tye) read and Говорите (ga-va-REE-tye) speak. A handful of verbs are irregular and simply have to be learned: дай give, ешь eat, пей drink, стой stand, поезжай go by vehicle. Aspect then does a second job in commands, which Spanish and English rarely make visible. An imperfective command invites someone to begin or to do something as a process, while a perfective command asks for one specific completed action. Cornell's example is exact: a host welcoming a guest says Снимайте пальто, садитесь (snee-MAY-tye pal-TO, sa-DEE-tyes) — take off your coat, have a seat, because a guest is being invited rather than directed; a doctor says Снимите рубашку и сядьте на стол (snee-MEE-tye roo-BASH-koo ee SYAD-tye na stol) — take off your shirt and sit on the table, because he wants those specific actions carried through. Obligation uses a different device again. Должен (DOL-zhen) is a short adjective that agrees with the person, who stays in the nominative: Я должна работать (ya dal-ZHNA ra-BO-tat) — I have to work. Надо and нужно (NA-da, NOOZH-na) are predicative words that put the person in the dative, as in Мне надо работать. Spanish tener que covers both, so the distinction has to be learned deliberately.
lessons.example: Ask the same person to do the same thing in four ways and watch the aspect and the politeness shift. Imperfective invitation: Садитесь, пожалуйста (sa-DEE-tyes, pa-ZHA-loos-ta) — please have a seat, which in Russian sounds like an open invitation to settle down. Perfective instruction: Сядьте сюда (SYAD-tye syoo-DA) — sit down here, which asks for one specific movement to one specific spot. Singular to a friend: Сядь сюда. Written note: Сядьте, пожалуйста, на этот стул (SYAD-tye, pa-ZHA-loos-ta, na EH-tat stool) — please sit on this chair. Now put obligation beside the commands: Тебе надо позвонить маме (tee-BYE NA-da paz-va-NEET MA-mye) — you have to phone mum, with the person in the dative, against Ты должна позвонить маме (ty dal-ZHNA paz-va-NEET MA-mye) — you have to phone mum, with the person nominative and the short adjective agreeing with her. Read all six aloud, then say for each whether it invites, instructs, or states an obligation, because that label decides both the verb form and the case of the person.
lessons.question: How do you express 'you have to phone your mother' in two structurally different ways, and what changes between them?
lessons.answer: Тебе надо позвонить маме puts the person in the dative with the predicative надо, while Ты должна позвонить маме keeps the person nominative and uses the short adjective должна, which agrees with her.
lessons.distractor: Ты надо позвонить маме is the plain version, because надо takes the nominative whenever the person is expressed by a pronoun.
lessons.correction: Надо never takes a nominative person: it is a predicative word like холодно, so the person it concerns stands in the dative, which is why Тебе надо is right and Ты надо is not. The alternative construction is the short adjective должна in the feminine, and there the person is the grammatical subject in the nominative, so the short adjective must agree in gender and number. Choose by deciding whether you want a person-centred statement with a subject or a subjectless statement with a dative experiencer; both are standard, and they differ in emphasis rather than in strength.

depth.definitions: The imperative is the mood of commands and requests, formed in Russian from the non-past stem with -и, -ь, or -й, plus -те for a polite or plural addressee. Aspect is the choice between an imperfective verb that views an action as ongoing, repeated, or merely begun and a perfective verb that views it as a single bounded whole. Obligation can be expressed with the short adjective должен, which agrees with a nominative subject, or with the predicatives надо and нужно, which take a dative person and an infinitive. A short adjective is a form that functions as a predicate, carrying is or are without a verb in the present.
depth.mechanism: Aspect in commands is not decoration; it changes what you are asking for. Cornell explains the politeness effect directly: an imperfective imperative sounds friendlier in a host-and-guest situation because it does not tell the other person to complete something, only to start doing it. The same source notes that some verbs cannot be used in the polite imperfective form at all, since their meaning precludes it, and gives Отстань от меня as perfective only, while it also records the opposite extreme, that infinitives are used for the strongest commands, as Сидеть! does in dog training. Two limits follow. First, the politeness contrast is a strong tendency tied to particular situations rather than a fixed social rule, so the same imperative can sound neutral in one setting and brusque in another. Second, negation interacts with aspect in a way this lesson deliberately does not reduce to a rule: Cornell notes that imperfective is the natural choice when the meaning is did not even start, while perfective is used when something was attempted and failed, and calls it a rough rule of thumb rather than a grammatical restriction.
depth.secondExample: A short exchange that mixes requests and obligations in three sentences. — Позвони мне, пожалуйста, когда приедешь (paz-va-NEE mnye, pa-ZHA-loos-ta, kag-DA pree-YE-desh) — call me please when you arrive: a singular perfective command for one specific action. — Хорошо, но мне нужно сначала купить билеты (kha-ra-SHO, no mnye NOOZH-na sna-CHA-la koo-PEET bee-LYE-ty) — all right, but I need to buy tickets first: a dative obligation with the infinitive. — Тебе не надо покупать их сегодня (tee-BYE nye NA-da pa-koo-PAT eekh see-VOD-nya) — you do not have to buy them today: negation of надо, which in Russian is ambiguous between must not and need not, with must not the more usual reading; the unambiguous need not is expressed as Ты можешь не покупать их сегодня. That ambiguity is a genuine trap for a literal translator and is handled properly in the next lesson.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first uses the wrong imperative ending, most often -й on a consonant stem, as in читать-style patterns applied to говорить. The second forgets -те when speaking politely to one person, which sounds as though you are addressing a child or a close friend. The third mixes the obligation constructions and produces Ты надо работать or Мне должна работать. The fourth treats negation of надо as if it were exactly like English must not or need not without noticing the ambiguity. Diagnose by naming the function first: is this a general invitation, a specific instruction, a request, or a statement of obligation? Then choose aspect, ending, and construction in that order.
depth.application: Optional practice: write five instructions for a routine you know well, such as leaving the flat in the morning, mixing at least two imperfective invitations and two perfective instructions, one polite form with -те, and one irregular imperative. Then rewrite three of them as obligations using надо with a dative person, and one of those using должен with a nominative subject. Model response for one line: Закрой окно, пожалуйста; потом тебе надо выключить свет (zak-ROY ak-NO, pa-ZHA-loos-ta; pa-TOM tee-BYE NA-da VY-klyoo-cheet svyet) — close the window please; then you have to switch off the light. Self-review checks four things: the ending matches the stem's stress and shape, -те is present when the addressee is plural or politely singular, aspect matches invitation versus instruction, and the obligation construction keeps the person in the right case. The task is nonblocking.
depth.summary: Imperatives are built from the non-past stem with -и, -ь, or -й and take -те for polite or plural address, with a small irregular set that must be memorised. Aspect turns a command into either an open invitation or a specific instruction, and negative commands follow a tendency rather than a strict rule. Obligation divides into a subject-centred construction with должен and a subjectless dative construction with надо or нужно, and Spanish tener que hides the difference.
